messages.author: 7d6a5c272d24acfa
messages.subject: bivariate normal-gamma distribution in stan
parts:
Hi all,

Edit: the previous code attached is my older version and has a typo. It is now fixed.

   I have a trouble with bivariate normal-gamma distribution in stan.

I wrote a simple code to sample random numbers based on bivariate normla-gamma distribution for my applications.

The following is my stan code and compiled in Ubuntu 13.10.

transformed data
{
   real mu;
   real<lower=0> kappa;
   real<lower=1> alpha;
   real<lower=0> beta;
   mu     <- -4.3;
   kappa  <-  3.1;
   alpha  <-  1.1;
   beta   <-  0.5;
}
parameters
{
   real<lower=0> lambda;
   real x;        
}
transformed parameters
{
   real<lower=0> sigma;
   sigma <- 1/sqrt(lambda*kappa);
}
model
{
   // Normal-Gamma distribution
   increment_log_prob(   gamma_log(lambda,alpha,beta)
                       + normal_log(x,mu,sigma)
                     );
}

I ran the executable with 

./normal-gamma.exe sample thin=10 num_warmup=1000000 num_samples=10000000

and I got a slightly off value which is

lambda = 2.251 with MCSE 2.323e-3

which is supposed to be 2.200 according to wikipedia.

Could anyone point me what is wrong with my code? Thank you for your help and kindness.

Note: My notation is based on this paper.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] bivariate normal-gamma distribution in stan
parts:
I would check that

a) the model's converging properly,

b) you're using the same parameterization of gamma (or should
that be inverse gamma?), and

c) whatever you're checking against is giving you the posterior
mean, not the posterior mode.

Could you include the Wikipedia reference?

Also, it's more efficient to use the sampling statements where
possible, replacing

> increment_log_prob( gamma_log(lambda,alpha,beta)
> + normal_log(x,mu,sigma)
> );

with

lambda ~ gamma(alpha,beta);
x ~ normal(mu,sigma);

The reason is that the sampling statement versions drop all
the unnecessary normalizing constants. Of course, if you need
those, then you need to use the increment_log_prob form.

Also, it's probably easier to break the increments apart,
as

increment_log_prob(gamma_log(lambda,alpha,beta));
increment_log_prob(normal_log(x,mu,sigma));

It's also a bit more efficient because increment_log_prob
uses an accumulator whereas the addition operator adds a new
node to the expression tree for auto-diff.

- Bob

messages.author: 7d6a5c272d24acfa
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] bivariate normal-gamma distribution in stan
parts:
Hi Bob,


Edit: fixed some typos.


   Thank you for your quick response.

The following uses Wikipedia notation for convenience (sorry for this confusion).

Here are links to wikipedia.
http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal-gamma_distribution
http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal-inverse-gamma_distribution
a) the model's converging properly,
I have run the model several times and I got an almost same answer and R_hat = 1.000, so I thought it converged well.
b) you're using the same parameterization of gamma (or should that be inverse gamma?), and

For normal distribution with unknown mean and unknown precision, normal-gamma is a conjugate prior. For unknown mean and unknown variance, normal-inverse-gamma is a conjugate prior. They are actually just parameter transformations.

I am interested in normal-gamma, but I can switch to normal-inverse-gamma for covenience.
c) whatever you're checking against is giving you the posterior mean, not the posterior mode.
Yes, I checked againt mean not mode. I should have checked the mode, too. I will check it when I get back to my office.

Also, it's more efficient to use the sampling statements where 
possible, replacing

>    increment_log_prob(   gamma_log(tau,alpha,beta) 
>                        + normal_log(x,mu,sigma) 
>                      ); 
with 
  tau ~ gamma(alpha,beta); 
  x ~ normal(mu,sigma); 

I understand your point, but I fully do not understand 

  tau ~ gamma(alpha,beta); 
  x ~ normal(mu,sigma); 

is correct or not (but both of them returned almost same answers). I saw many BUGS people said that the same approach works with normal-inverse-gamma in BUGS, and it returned the expected answer in BUGS. However, I still not sure it is really correct way in the Gibbs sampler because given x, Normal-Gamma (or Normal-Inverse-Gamma) is not Gamma (or Inverse-Gamma). Given x, Normal-Gamma is gamma times extra tau terms from normal distribution. I may misunderstand how BUGS works, tho.


Anyway, as you can see from Wikipedia Normal-Gamma, we can factorize Normal-Gamma with

NG(x,tau|alpha,beta,mu,lambda) = gamma(tau|alpha,beta) normal(x|mu,tau,lambda)

So, I reparameterized tau*lambda = 1/sigma^2 which is defined in

transformed parameters
{
   real<lower=0> sigma;

sigma = 1/sqrt(lambda*tau);
}

and I took log resulted in

   increment_log_prob(   gamma_log(lambda,alpha,beta)
                       + normal_log(x,mu,sigma)

but this did not return a correct mean for lambda, but x is fine.

I should have tried to write them out explicitly without using gamma_log and normal_log.

I will check it when I get back to my office...
Thank you for your help and kindness.

Shota

2014年3月13日木曜日 20時33分02秒 UTC+9 Bob Carpenter:
I would check that

a) the model's converging properly,

b) you're using the same parameterization of gamma (or should
that be inverse gamma?), and

c) whatever you're checking against is giving you the posterior
mean, not the posterior mode.

Could you include the Wikipedia reference?

Also, it's more efficient to use the sampling statements where
possible, replacing

>    increment_log_prob(   gamma_log(lambda,alpha,beta)
>                        + normal_log(x,mu,sigma)
>                      );

with

  lambda ~ gamma(alpha,beta);
  x ~ normal(mu,sigma);

The reason is that the sampling statement versions drop all
the unnecessary normalizing constants.  Of course, if you need
those, then you need to use the increment_log_prob form.

Also, it's probably easier to break the increments apart,
as

  increment_log_prob(gamma_log(lambda,alpha,beta));
  increment_log_prob(normal_log(x,mu,sigma));

It's also a bit more efficient because increment_log_prob
uses an accumulator whereas the addition operator adds a new
node to the expression tree for auto-diff.

- Bob

parts:
Hi Bob,

   I have attached a simplest stan-code (alpha = 1.1 and beta = 0.5).

According to Wikipedia (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal-gamma_distribution),  an analytic mean, mode and variance are given by

x:
  Mean:x
  Mode:x
  StdDev:sqrt(beta/(lambda*(alpha-1)))
tau:
  Mean:alpha/beta
  Mode:(alpha-0.5)/beta
  StdDev:sqrt(alpha/beta^2)


Case 1: mu = -4.3, alpha = 1.1, beta = 0.5
Expected Values:
x:
  Mean:-4.3
  Mode:-4.3
  StdDev:sqrt(50/31) ~ 1.270...
tau:
  Mean:2.2
  Mode:1.2
  Variance:4.4

Case 1 Results:
x:
  Mean: -4.301 (OK)
  Mode:-4.300 (OK)
  StdDev:1.033 (slightly off due to tau)
tau:
  Mean: 2.246 (2% off. considering MCSE = 5.262e-3, this error is a bit large)
  Mode: 1.200 (Exact)
  StdDev:2.133 (off a half an expected value)

Case 2:mu = -4.3, alpha = 9.0, beta = 4.0 (the code is not attached.)
Expected Values:
x:
  Mean:-4.3
  Mode:-4.3
  StdDev:sqrt(155)/31 ~ 0.401609
tau:
  Mean:2.25
  Mode:2.125
  StdDev:0.5625

Case 2 Results:
x:
  Mean:-4.300 (OK)
  Mode:-4.300 (OK)
  StdDev:0.3991 (close enough)
tau:
  Mean:2.251 (close enough)
  Mode:2.125 (OK)
  StdDev:0.7438 (a bit off)

To reproduce the results, I used the following arguments:

./normal-gamma-version1.exe sample num_warmup=10000 num_samples=1000000 random seed=324393 init=normal-gamma-version1.init.R

As a note, a gamma distribution with alpha = 1.1 and beta = 0.5 is a heavy-tale distribution (this could be a reason). 2% error seems to be small, but the normal-gamma is a conjugate prior to the lognormal distribution and 2% error is deadly significant to my case...

Thank you for your help and kindness.

Shota

Raw numbers are meaningless by themselves; at the very least
you should be looking at (mean - expected) / MCSE.  And if you
expect that a heavy tail is possibly to blame then increase the
target acceptance probability.
